title: Pregnancy-associated cardiac complications
abstract: Cardiovascular disease has become the most common cause of maternal mortality in the United States and non-obstetric cause of maternal mortality worldwide. Pregnancy profoundly alters maternal physiology and creates multiple maternal vulnerabilities, especially but not uniquely in women with preexisting cardiac disease. Common cardiac conditions represented in this patient population include arrhythmias, cardiomyopathies, and valvular heart disease, putting women at risk for numerous adverse events of pregnancy, including pre-eclampsia, heart failure, preterm delivery, and small-for-gestational-age babies. These complications often foretell long-term maternal cardiovascular risks and are also highly influenced by socioeconomic circumstances. To address these issues, cardio-obstetrics has emerged as a diverse and growing field spanning multiple medical specialties. Due to the breadth of pathology, a multidisciplinary Cardio-Obstetrics management team strategy is crucial. We review here common cardiac pathologies and their management throughout the peripartum period.

title: Mucoadhesive recombinant human catalase for dry eye disease: From protein engineering to first-in-human study
abstract: Background Oxidative stress caused by excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) plays a key role in the progression of dry eye disease (DED), yet no approved DED therapy directly eliminates ROS. Here, we develop an antioxidant biologic with enhanced ocular-surface retention by thiol engineering of recombinant human catalase (hCAT) as a new ROS-scavenging eye drop therapy for DED. Methods Thiolated hCAT (hCAT-SH) was characterized for activity, stability, mucin interaction, and ocular retention. Efficacy, mechanism, and safety were evaluated in mouse, rabbit, and rat studies, followed by a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled first-in-human trial in 30 patients with DED. Findings With formulation optimization, hCAT-SH maintained enzymatic activity and formulation stability, while exhibiting enhanced mucin binding and prolonged corneal retention. In mouse DED models, hCAT-SH reduced oxidative stress, accelerated epithelial repair, restored tear secretion, and modulated inflammatory and barrier-repair pathways distinct from cyclosporine. In rabbits, exposure remained predominantly ocular with favorable repeated-dose tolerability. Clinically, 0.1 mg/mL hCAT-SH significantly improved corneal fluorescein staining, reduced tear cytokine levels and corneal dendritic cell density versus placebo, and raised no treatment-related safety concerns. Conclusions hCAT-SH is a carrier-free, long-retained H 2 O 2 -scavenging biologic, with integrated preclinical and first-in-human evidence supporting further development as a new DED drug. Funding National Natural Science Foundation of China; National Technology Innovation Center for Biopharmaceuticals; Jiangsu Key R&D Program; National Key R&D Program of China; Shanghai "Dawn" Program; Shanghai Science and Technology Innovation Action Plans; Shanghai Municipal Commission of Health; Shanghai High-Quality Development Plan for Science and Technology Industry; and Macao FDCT.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure in the periconceptional period and adverse obstetric outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis assesses whether exposure to glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) during pregnancy or the periconceptional period is associated with adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes. METHODS: Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for observational studies comparing pregnancies exposed and unexposed to GLP-1 RAs within 6 months before a positive pregnancy test. Outcomes included miscarriage, intrauterine death, congenital anomalies, preterm birth (PTB), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), fetal growth restriction (FGR), small for gestational age (SGA), large for gestational age (LGA), and excess gestational weight gain. Random-effects meta-analyses and subgroup analyses by indication were performed. FINDINGS: Ten studies included 2,118,215 women, of whom 8,325 were exposed and 2,109,890 were unexposed. Pooled estimates did not show a clearly detectable increase in miscarriage or intrauterine death, congenital anomalies, preterm birth, HDP, gestational diabetes, abnormal fetal growth, or excess gestational weight gain. A lower pooled estimate for preeclampsia was observed (odds ratio [OR]: 0.87, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78-0.98; p = 0.02), but this was based on two datasets and should be interpreted cautiously. Subgroup analyses showed no clearly detectable differences by indication. The exposure-window sensitivity analysis, covering 90 days before conception through the end of the first trimester, used the same four studies as the primary congenital-malformation analysis and therefore was not independent. CONCLUSION: Available observational evidence did not identify a clearly detectable increase in adverse maternal or perinatal outcomes following periconceptional exposure to GLP-1 RAs. However, these findings do not establish safety because of heterogeneity, residual confounding, and limited datasets. FUNDING: None.

title: Q&A with Mihaela van der Schaar
abstract: Mihaela van der Schaar is John Humphrey Plummer Professor of Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence and Medicine, at the University of Cambridge, where she leads the van der Schaar Lab, directs the Cambridge Centre for AI in Medicine, and serves as Chief AI Scientist at the Francis Crick Institute. An IEEE Fellow since 2009 and Fellow of the Royal Society since 2024, she has received major honors including the Johann Anton Merck Award, Cambridge's Oon Prize, and an NSF CAREER Award. She holds 35 US patents, contributed to 45 international standards, earned 3 ISO Awards, and was named the UK's most-cited female AI researcher.

title: MAIT cells show promise as an immunotherapy tool with both adaptive and innate characteristics
abstract: May unconventional MAIT cells be an effective innovative immunotherapy tool against liver cancer? This question is addressed by Yang and colleagues in this issue of Med. 1 Their findings with adoptive transfer of expanded human MAIT cells to cancer xenograft mouse models suggest that these cells may hold greater promise in the cancer field than previously thought.

title: When the standard changes during the trial: Reflections on targeted therapy in FGFR2-rearranged cholangiocarcinoma
ASTRUM-006 and the changing landscape of perioperative therapy for gastric cancer
abstract: ASTRUM-006 provides phase 3 evidence that perioperative immune checkpoint inhibition improves event-free survival with Asian SOX-based chemotherapy in PD-L1-positive gastric cancer. Its postoperative chemotherapy-sparing strategy is attractive, although unmasking, event adjudication, and non-R0 or occult metastatic disease warrant consideration. The study nevertheless broadens the perioperative treatment framework and provides an important platform for refining patient selection and postoperative treatment intensity.

title: Renal rescue in myeloma: How deep does the hematologic response need to be?
abstract: The choice of first-line therapy is exceptionally challenging when multiple myeloma is associated with advanced renal failure. In this issue of Med, Xiao and colleagues report on results from a randomized phase 2 study 1 indicating that the pomalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone triplet leads to better myeloma disease control, thereby increasing renal function after four cycles.

title: Trunk-mediated spinal cord stimulation: A step toward clinical implementation after spinal cord injury
abstract: In this issue of Med, Agnesi et al., show that residual trunk movements after spinal cord injury can modulate the effects of epidural spinal cord stimulation (SCS) to enable participants to volitionally initiate and control stepping. 1 This trunk-mediated interface offers a practical strategy for bringing epidural SCS one step closer to widespread clinical adoption.

title: Genome editing for hereditary angioedema: A landmark trial and important unanswered questions
abstract: Hereditary angioedema is a bradykinin-mediated genetic disorder increasingly controlled with effective long-term prophylaxis. In a phase 3 trial, a single dose of lonvoguran ziclumeran, an in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 therapy targeting KLKB1, significantly reduced attack rates. This approach represents a highly promising therapeutic strategy for HAE. However, it also raises important questions that require further investigation.

title: Early detection of gastric cancer using DNA features in red blood cells, with multicenter validation
abstract: Background Early detection of gastric cancer (GC) is limited by invasive endoscopy and poor sensitivity of blood-based biomarkers. Red blood cells (RBCs), the most abundant cells in the circulation, are anucleate but can retain DNA remnants that have been associated with pathological stress. Here, we report a non-invasive strategy for GC detection based on genome-wide profiling of DNA remnants retained in RBCs (rbcDNA). Methods We performed shallow whole-genome sequencing of rbcDNA from 1-2 mL of peripheral blood of 865 individuals, including 434 treatment-naive GC patients and 431 non-GC controls with benign gastric conditions. In the discovery cohort, we identified 1,000 reproducible rbcDNA read-depth features distinguishing GC from non-cancer states. A machine learning classifier based on dimensionally reduced GC-associated rbcDNA features was trained in the discovery cohort (n = 435), with the cutoff fixed at 90% specificity, and evaluated in a test cohort (n = 109) and three independent multicenter validation cohorts (n = 321). Findings The classifier achieved the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 84% in nested cross-validation of the discovery cohort and 95% in the test cohort. Across three hospital-based multicenter validation cohorts, performance remained consistent, with 83%-90% overall sensitivity and 82%-89% sensitivity for stage I GC. Additionally, the classifier distinguished early-stage GC from precancerous lesions and other tumors and detected ∼80% of GC cases negative for tumor markers. Conclusions These findings demonstrate the potential of rbcDNA as a non-invasive biomarker for early-stage GC detection. Funding This work was supported by the Key Research and Development Program of Zhejiang Province (2026C02A1176 and 2024C03170).

title: Cancer plasticity and histological transformation as adaptive resistance mechanisms in precision oncology
abstract: The advent of precision oncology has brought substantial advancements in cancer therapy, yet it has been accompanied by equally complex resistance mechanisms. Among these mechanisms, histological transformations can compromise the effectiveness of targeted therapies, resulting in a loss of clinical benefit following initial success. Understanding these evolutionary processes is crucial for developing the next generation of cancer treatments that can effectively combat resistance. This review examines histological transformation as a key mechanism of resistance to anticancer therapies, driven by various forms of tumor plasticity, and explores into the underlying processes and mechanisms that drive these changes. We also discuss how precision oncology and an appreciation of cancer plasticity can be leveraged to overcome histological transformation and lead to improved patient outcomes.

title: Endovascular treatment for ischemic stroke due to distal medium vessel occlusions: A nationwide multicenter registry
abstract: BACKGROUND: The effectiveness and safety of endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke attributable to distal medium vessel occlusion (DMVO) remain uncertain. This study aimed to compare the effectiveness and safety of EVT plus standard medical treatment (SMT) versus SMT alone in patients with DMVO. METHODS: This nationwide multicenter registry included patients with DMVO presenting within 24 h of last known well at 116 sites in China between 2023 and 2025. The primary outcome was freedom from disability (modified Rankin Scale score of 0-1) at 90 days. Safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) within 48 h and 90-day mortality. The primary analysis was conducted using inverse probability of treatment weighting. FINDINGS: Among 2,524 patients, 1,564 received EVT plus SMT, and 960 received SMT alone. EVT plus SMT was associated with a higher rate of freedom from disability at 90 days compared with SMT alone (adjusted risk ratio [aRR], 1.15; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.02-1.29; adjusted risk difference, 4.36%; 95% CI, 1.73%-6.99%). However, EVT plus SMT was associated with an increased risk of sICH (aRR, 4.03; 95% CI, 2.46-6.59). Mortality at 90 days did not differ significantly between the groups (aRR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.81-1.16). CONCLUSIONS: In patients with DMVO, EVT plus SMT was associated with a modestly higher rate of freedom from disability at 90 days but an increased risk of sICH. FUNDING: National Natural Science Foundation of China (82425021, 82571498, and 82271349), Natural Science Foundation of Chongqing (CSTB2024NSCQ-MSX0359 and CSTB2024NSCQ-KJFZMSX0063), and Chongqing Technology Innovation and Application Development Project (CSTB2022TIAD-KPX0160).

title: Tumor DNA methylation subtypes and expression levels of CFISH predict response and overall survival to immunochemotherapy
abstract: BACKGROUND: Predicting patient response to immunochemotherapy is vital but challenging and poorly studied in the (neo)adjuvant setting. We showed that tumor monocyte content (TMC) predicts overall survival of advanced esophageal cancer (OC) in response to immunochemotherapy. We report clinical outcomes of 35 operable OC patients receiving ICI-based therapy and molecular profiling of the unique phase-2 LUD2015-005 trial treating 73 OC patients (38 advanced/inoperable and 35 operable) in the (neo)adjuvant setting. METHODS: LUD2015-005 trial patients were treated with 4-week immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-only before combination with standard of care. Paired and longitudinally collected biopsies of tumor and multiple adjacent normal sites were bi-dissected to extract DNA and RNA. Whole-genome, methylome, single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing data generated from the entire LUD2015-005 cohort were used for cell-deconvolution and data integration analysis. FINDINGS: T cells upon ICI+ chemotherapy/chemoradiotherapy. We identified five DNA-methylation subtypes with distinct TiME and a TMC-related five-gene signature CFISH (CXCL8, FCN1, IFI30, SLC11A1, and HLA-DRA) as highly predictive biomarkers of overall survival in OC and beyond. CONCLUSIONS: These findings highlight the importance of the myeloid compartment in ICI response and the potential of CFISH and tumor DNA methylation in patient stratification for immunochemotherapy. FUNDING: This work is mainly funded by Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, CRUK Grants A21998 and C30423/A2541, and NIHR Oxford Biomedical Research Center. AstraZeneca UK Limited provided durvalumab and tremelimumab for LUD2015-005.

title: Interpretation of genome sequencing results in children with complex neuromotor phenotypes
abstract: Background Although genetic diseases cause at least 30% of neuromotor disorders, genome sequencing is not routinely used for diagnosis in such patients. We assessed the diagnostic value in children with complex neuromotor phenotypes. Methods We performed trio genome sequencing in 108 children with complex neuromotor phenotypes in 100 families. Genetic disease was diagnosed by a multidisciplinary clinical research team on the basis of each child's complete medical history, clinical course, family history, physical examination, imaging studies, and all other laboratory test results, as well as the findings on genome sequencing. Genetic variants that were suspected of being disease causing were subjected to orthogonal confirmation in a clinically accredited laboratory, which classified the variants it reported according to the ACMG/AMP guidelines. Findings We diagnosed genetic diseases that explained the neuromotor phenotype in 53 of the 100 families studied. Almost all of these children had intellectual disability, a seizure disorder, and/or autism spectrum disorder in addition to neuromotor impairment. An important factor contributing to this high diagnostic rate was the use of each patient's complete clinical phenotype, instead of a "molecular diagnosis" based only on the ACMG/AMP variant classification. Conclusions Our findings demonstrate that complex neuromotor phenotypes in children are usually manifestations of a more generalized neurodevelopmental disorder and that the ACMG/AMP classification alone is insufficient to establish or exclude a causal relationship between a genomic variant and a suspected genetic disease. Funding Canadian Institutes of Health Research, British Columbia Children's Hospital Foundation, and Michael Smith Health Research BC.

title: Systemic antitumor responses to hypofractionated radiotherapy plus Poly(I:C) in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma: A phase 2 trial
abstract: Background The abscopal effect, regression of unirradiated tumors after localized radiotherapy, is rare. Whether hypofractionated radiotherapy (HFRT) plus the innate immune agonist polyinosinic-polycytidylic acid [Poly(I:C)] amplifies systemic antitumor immunity in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma is unclear. Methods In this single-arm, phase 2 trial (ChiCTR2100053441), 37 patients received HFRT plus subcutaneous Poly(I:C); 33 were response evaluable. Outcomes were compared with 33 propensity score-matched patients treated with HFRT alone. The primary endpoint was the objective response rate per RECIST v.1.1; secondary endpoints included progression-free survival, overall survival, and safety; and abscopal response was prespecified. Mechanisms were explored by single-cell RNA sequencing and flow cytometry in patients and by CD8 depletion and CD28 blockade in mice. Findings HFRT plus Poly(I:C) was well tolerated; it was associated with a higher objective response rate (54.5% vs. 21.2%; p = 0.011) and abscopal response rate (45.0% vs. 10.5%; p = 0.042) as well as longer progression-free survival (8.4 vs. 4.6 months; adjusted hazard ratio = 0.542; p = 0.042) and overall survival (not reached vs. 13.6 months; adjusted hazard ratio = 0.386; p = 0.011) vs. HFRT alone. The progression-free survival benefit was also higher in patients concurrently receiving tyrosine kinase inhibitors (p for interaction = 0.013). Peripheral CD8 + CD28 + T cell expansion correlated with abscopal tumor control; in mice, CD8 + T cells and CD28 co-stimulation were required for this effect. Conclusions HFRT plus Poly(I:C) showed promising systemic antitumor activity with manageable safety in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, with CD8 + CD28 + T cells as an immune correlate of response. These exploratory findings warrant confirmation in randomized trials. Funding The National Natural Science Foundation of China.

title: Restoration of volitional lower-limb movement after motor-complete spinal cord injury with brain-spine interface
abstract: Background Spinal cord injury (SCI) interrupts volitional control of lower limbs. Brain-spine interfaces (BSIs), which decode cortical motor intent to trigger epidural electrical stimulation (EES), can provide an artificial pathway linking the brain to spinal motor circuits. Reported benefit, however, has been confined to participants who already retain substantial motor function, leaving unresolved whether those with little or no motor function can benefit, how soon, and how consistently. Methods Three individuals with motor-complete SCI were enrolled in a registered trial (ChiCTR2500095359). None could stand or step with braces, walking aids, or physical assistance. Each received one depth electrode per hemisphere in the lower-limb motor cortex and an epidural paddle spanning the L1-S2 nerve roots. The participants underwent 2-3 weeks of closed-loop BSI training. Findings The interface restored brain-controlled volitional lower-limb movement on the first postoperative day in all three participants and assisted walking with body-weight support followed within 2 weeks. Over the training period, all three developed coordinated remodeling across cortical, spinal, and muscular levels, with thigh muscle volume increasing by 4.9% on average. Conclusions These findings widen the conditions under which a BSI is known to work. It can take effect rapidly in participants with no volitional lower-limb movement to build on, at a low implant demand, and consistently across all three participants. Funding This work was supported by the National Key R&D Program of China (Disruptive Technology Innovation; grant no. 2025YFF1501400) and the Shanghai Municipal Science and Technology Major Project (grant no. 25DP3200100).

title: Bacteria inside kidney tumors associate with myeloid inflammation and disease progression: A TRACERx Renal study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intratumoral bacteria are increasingly recognized as active contributors to neutrophil-driven inflammation and disease progression in solid tumors. Yet, in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), where myeloid inflammation is a key feature of aggressive disease, live bacterial presence, their intratumoral distribution, and interaction with the tumor microenvironment remain unexplored. METHODS: We genetically characterized the microbiome of primary ccRCC tumors across two independent cohorts (TRACERx: 616 samples, 143 patients; The Cancer Genome Atlas [TCGA]: 511 samples and patients), confirming live bacterial presence through culture. Multi-regional sampling enabled within-tumor analysis of bacterial distribution. Associations with the tumor microenvironment were explored at scale using bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) across both cohorts and corroborated in depth through spatial transcriptomics and in vitro infection assays. FINDINGS: ). Both across and within tumors, Cutibacterium accumulation associated with neutrophil recruitment and myeloid inflammation. In vitro, Cutibacterium induced sustained expression of neutrophil-attracting chemokines in macrophages, recapitulating patient tumor findings. CONCLUSIONS: These findings establish intratumoral bacteria as novel prognostic components of the ccRCC tumor microenvironment and suggest an active role in shaping local myeloid inflammation, laying the groundwork for investigating their potential as therapeutic targets. FUNDING: This work was supported by the Francis Crick Institute (Cancer Research UK, MRC, Wellcome Trust). TRACERx Renal is funded by Cancer Research UK (C50947/A18176).

title: Metabolic endotyping for mechanism-informed Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease trials
abstract: Metabolically targeted therapies for Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease have yielded mixed results despite convergent evidence implicating three interconnected axes of metabolic dysfunction: insulin signaling, cellular bioenergetics, and lipid-lysosomal biology. We argue that this pattern partly reflects a trial-design problem: therapeutics such as glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, terazosin, and stearoyl-CoA desaturase inhibitors generally have been tested in biologically unselected populations, with endpoints often distal to the targeted mechanism. We propose as a testable hypothesis that a metabolic endotype-a measurable, biomarker-supported pattern of metabolic dysfunction-spans subsets of both diseases and that failure to enrich for this endotype could dilute therapeutic signals in all-comer trials. We outline a modular four-tier framework integrating prodromal risk, metabolic vulnerability, pathway-specific confirmation, and mechanistic deep phenotyping to make Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease trials more interpretable and therapeutically informative.
